title: Micah: under the fig tree (Micah 4:4)
hook: each under their vine and fig tree, "and none shall make them afraid"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah answered a bidding war of rams and rivers of oil with three verbs. Your line was justly, mercy, humbly. Which of the three came easiest? Today, Micah again, and a picture of peace small enough to sit in. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

A fig tree throws real shade. Its leaves are broad, and on a hot afternoon the ground under one is cool and green. Micah's fourth chapter starts enormous. The mountain of the LORD's house raised above the hills, and peoples streaming toward it to learn. Then the line about swords, in the King James: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks." Nation shall not lift up a sword against nation. That's the view from very high up. And then Micah does something unexpected. He comes all the way down, from nations to one person, sitting in one patch of shade.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, AND PEOPLES STREAMING.` → `SWORDS INTO PLOWSHARES.` → `DOWN TO ONE PATCH OF SHADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid." Read it slowly, because every piece is doing work. Sit. Not marching, not working, not standing guard. Sitting is what you do when you don't have to watch the road. His vine, his fig tree. His own. Not rented, not borrowed, not taken from someone else. The picture is of someone who expects to stay. And then the last phrase. In Hebrew it's short: ve'ein macharid, and none shall make them tremble. That's how Micah measures peace. Not by a treaty, not by a map with no battles on it, but by whether a person sitting in their own yard has anything left to flinch at. The swords are gone, yes. But the vision isn't finished until the fear is gone too. The picture has a past in the Bible. In the book of Kings, in Solomon's days, Judah and Israel are said to have lived safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree. So Micah's hope reaches back to a remembered good time and promises it again, for everyone. The verse ends with a signature: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it. And that brings it close to home. What makes people afraid is often small and close. A tone of voice. A door slammed. A person who might laugh at you. The vision is as big as the nations. Its last line fits in a kitchen.
screen: `SIT: NOBODY HAS TO WATCH THE ROAD.` · `HIS OWN VINE, HIS OWN FIG TREE.` · then, large: `AND NONE SHALL MAKE THEM AFRAID.` · then: `THE LAST LINE FITS IN A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: make someone feel safe. Start with yourself. First, notice anything in you that's braced: shoulders up, jaw tight, waiting for the next thing. Let a little of it go, the way you would sitting in shade. Then bring to mind one person who might be braced around you. A child. A coworker who answers to you. A partner, a parent, a friend who seems careful lately. Ask what would let them sit easy in your company. A softer voice. A promise kept. Telling them plainly they're not in trouble. Choose one. If you pray, you can say Micah's line for them. The bell holds the time.
Micah. The prophet who brought the peace of nations down to one person under a vine and a fig tree, with nothing to be afraid of. Today's word.
Your line: none shall make them afraid. Today, be the reason one person flinches a little less: a gentler answer, a calmer text, a kept word. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read Micah among the Twelve, and the hope of each person under their own vine and fig tree is sung and quoted in Jewish life as a picture of peace without fear.

original.note: Hebrew: "and none makes them tremble," the last words of Micah's picture of peace.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line about gardens.
what it means: peace measured by whether one person, in their own yard, has anything left to fear.
what a scholar hears: an echo of Solomon's days in the book of Kings, promised again for everyone, after the swords-into-plowshares vision.
